Thomas made it to the shore at Sandy Point, his hands bleeding from the rope burns and his heart hammering. He did not fish past the Black Rocks again. And when his own children were old enough to listen, he told them the story his grandmother had told him, pressing their hands against the window each evening as the sun touched the horizon.
moral: The warnings of elders carry the weight of those who learned the hard way. Ignore them only if you are willing to become the next cautionary tale.

title: The Mocko Jumbie of Sandy Point
summary: During the Christmas Carnival season, a master stilt walker in Sandy Point channels the spirit of the Mocko Jumbie to protect the village from duppies and ill fortune.
full_text:
In Sandy Point, the old capital of Saint Kitts, the tradition of the Mocko Jumbie runs deeper than anywhere else on the island. The villagers say that the first Mocko Jumbie appeared in their village two centuries ago, when enslaved Africans brought the custom from the Gold Coast. Since then, Sandy Point has been the spiritual home of the stilt walker who guards the community.

Master Elroy was the finest Mocko Jumbie practitioner of his generation. He had learned from his uncle, who had learned from his father, and the knowledge passed through their hands like the grain of the wooden stilts themselves. Each November, as Carnival approached, Master Elroy would begin his preparations. He would carve new stilts from the heartwood of the mahogany tree, sanding them smooth with the patience of a man who understood that his work held lives.

The night before the first parade, Master Elroy performed his ritual alone in the yard behind his house. He dressed in the traditional costume, the long flowing gown of bright fabric, the conical hat that added another foot to his towering height, and the mask that concealed his face. He mounted the stilts and began to dance.

The villagers who lived nearby said the air changed when Master Elroy danced. The crickets fell silent. The night breeze held its breath. His movements were impossibly graceful for a man balanced on eight feet of wood, and as he danced, he seemed to grow taller, as though the stilts were not props but extensions of his body reaching toward the heavens.

'The Mocko Jumbie sees what we cannot see,' Master Elroy had told a young apprentice years before. 'He sees the duppies that linger at the edges. He sees the ill intentions that drift like smoke through the village. His height is his gift, and his dance is his shield.'

On the morning of the parade, the streets of Sandy Point filled with music and laughter. Steel bands hammered out rhythms that shook the shutters, and children ran between the legs of adults, chasing the colors of the costumes. Then Master Elroy appeared at the head of the procession, swaying on his stilts above the crowd, and the people parted like water.

He moved through the village in a trance of rhythm and balance, and wherever he passed, the old people said, the air grew lighter. Puppies that had been whimpering fell quiet. A woman who had been ill for weeks felt a warmth pass through her as the Mocko Jumbie danced above her doorway. Something unseen lifted from the village that day, carried away by the height and power of the dance.

When the parade ended and the sun set over the harbor, Master Elroy removed his mask and stepped down from the stilts. He was just a man again, sweating and tired, but the villagers looked at him differently. They saw what he carried, and they understood that some traditions endure because they are necessary.
moral: Some traditions survive slavery and colonialism because they carry power that no system can destroy. The Mocko Jumbie reminds us that protection can be found in the most beautiful and improbable forms.

title: The Green Lady and the Fisherman's Heart
summary: A grief-stricken fisherman climbs Mount Liamuiga at sunset and witnesses the Green Lady's flash, receiving a sign that love endures beyond loss.
full_text:
They say the Green Lady was once a woman named Aisha who lived in the village of Dieppe during the time when the French and British fought over Saint Kitts. She was beautiful in the way that caused men to forget their prudence, and she loved a fisherman named Raphael who sailed the waters between Saint Kitts and Nevis. Their love was simple and fierce, the kind that grows between two people who share the same sky every morning.

But the colonial masters would not permit it. Raphael was of one nation, Aisha of another, and the war between empires extended its petty hatreds into the hearts of those who had no stake in it. Raphael was sent away, and Aisha was promised to another. She climbed to the peak of Mount Liamuiga, the great volcano that watches over the island, and she wept for three days.

On the third evening, as the sun dipped below the Caribbean horizon, a light passed through Aisha and she was gone. But from that day forward, the people of Saint Kitts would sometimes see a brilliant green flash at the moment the sun touched the sea, and they knew it was the Green Lady, still searching, still loving, still burning with a devotion that death could not dim.

Decades later, an old fisherman named Dorian lost his wife, Marie, to a fever that swept through Basseterre in the wet season. He was not a young man, and the grief settled into his bones like the damp of the sea. He stopped fishing. He stopped eating with his neighbors. Each evening, he climbed the western ridge of the island where the sunset was unbroken by trees or buildings, and he sat on the same flat stone and watched the sun go down.

His neighbors said he was going mad with sorrow. But Dorian was not mad. He was looking for something.

One evening in October, when the air was clear and the horizon line was sharp as a blade, Dorian watched the sun sink into the sea. And just as the last sliver of light vanished, the sky erupted in green. It was not a gentle flash. It was a blaze, a column of emerald fire that split the horizon and turned the sea the color of jade.

Dorian felt something pass through him, not cold but warm, like the hand of someone who had been holding his all along. He did not see a woman. He did not hear a voice. But he understood, in a way that bypassed language entirely, that love does not end when a person does. It transforms. It finds new forms. It becomes light.

He climbed down the mountain and began to fish again. He ate with his neighbors and laughed at their stories. When people asked what had changed, he would say simply, 'I saw the Green Lady, and she told me what I needed to know.'

The old women of Basseterre nod when they hear this. They have their own stories of the Green Lady. Some have seen the flash themselves. They say she appears to those who need her most, and that her message is always the same: love is stronger than grief, and hope is never extinguished as long as the sun rises and sets over Saint Kitts.
moral: Love does not die with the beloved. It transforms and endures, and if you are patient and open, it will find a way to reach you, even as light.

title: The Duppy of Brimstone Hill
summary: A young soldier stationed at Brimstone Hill Fort ignores the old guard's warning about duppies and is visited by a restless spirit in the dead of night.
full_text:
Brimstone Hill rises from the western coast of Saint Kitts like a clenched fist, and the fortress at its summit has stood since the British carved it from the volcanic rock in the seventeenth century. The hill has seen more blood and suffering than most places on the island, and the Kittitians say that some of those who died there never left.

Corporal James was a young soldier newly assigned to the fort. He was fresh from training and full of the confidence that comes from knowing how to handle a rifle but not yet from knowing what a rifle has handled. The old guard, a sergeant named Baptiste who had served at the fort for twenty years, took one look at him and shook his head.

'You hear things at night up here,' Baptiste said on James's first evening. 'Footsteps on the ramparts when no one is walking. Voices in the magazine when it is locked and empty. Do not answer them. Do not call out a name. And if you hear knocking at your door after midnight, do not open it.'

James smiled and said he was not superstitious. Baptiste looked at him with the expression of a man who had seen things that superstition does not begin to cover, and he walked away without another word.

The first three nights were uneventful. James slept in the old quarters, a stone room with a single window that faced the sea. On the fourth night, he woke to the sound of footsteps on the stone floor above him. They were slow and deliberate, the steps of someone pacing. He lay still and listened. The footsteps stopped directly above his bed.

Then came the knocking. Three slow strikes on his door, evenly spaced, as though someone was testing whether he was awake. James sat up. The rational part of his mind suggested it was one of the other soldiers. The rest of him knew better. He did not call out. He did not open the door.

The knocking came again, harder this time, and with it came a voice. It was faint, muffled by the thick stone walls, but he could make out words. 'James. Open the door, James.' The voice sounded like his mother's.

His mother was alive, two islands away in Antigua, and had never set foot in Brimstone Hill. James understood then what Baptiste had meant. The duppy knew his name. It had reached into his memory and pulled the voice of the person he loved most, and it was using that voice to open the door.

He pressed a silver coin, a gift from his grandmother, against his chest and spoke through the door in the language Baptiste had taught him. 'I am not the one you are looking for. Go back to where you belong.'

The knocking stopped. The footsteps retreated. The silence that followed was so complete that James could hear his own heartbeat.

In the morning, Baptiste was waiting for him at the mess hall with a cup of strong coffee. He looked at James and nodded once. No words were needed. James had passed the test that every soldier at Brimstone Hill eventually faced, and he would never again dismiss the old stories as superstition.
moral: The dead have their own claims, and the living honor them not by opening every door but by knowing which ones must remain closed.

title: The Mermaids Who Saved Saint Kitts
summary: During a great storm that threatens to destroy the fishing fleet, the Black Rocks Mermaids reveal that they are not only destroyers but protectors of those who respect the sea.
full_text:
The old fishermen of Saint Kitts tell of a time when the sea turned against the island with a fury that had no name. It was not a hurricane, for the winds were not from the north. It was something older, a rage that rose from the deep water as though the ocean floor itself had opened. The waves were black and tall as houses, and they broke against the coast with a sound like thunder split in two.

The fishing fleet was out. All twelve boats, carrying nearly forty men, had set sail at dawn for the grounds east of Nevis. By midday the sky had turned the color of a bruise, and by afternoon the radio in the Basseterre harbor office crackled with desperate voices and then went silent.

On the shore at Black Rocks, the villagers gathered and watched the sea rage. Old Mama Vivienne, who was known throughout the village for her knowledge of the old stories, stood at the front of the crowd. She looked at the volcanic rocks where the mermaids were said to live, and she spoke to the water.

'You have taken many from us,' she said, her voice steady against the wind. 'But these are our sons and husbands and fathers. If you have any mercy, bring them home.'

The sea did not quiet. But Mama Vivienne's granddaughter, a girl named Soleil, noticed something. Among the black waves, near the jagged rocks where no boat should venture, there were shapes moving. They were pale against the dark water, and they moved with a speed and purpose that no human swimmer could match. The mermaids.

The villagers watched as the shapes dove and surfaced, dove and surfaced, and each time they surfaced, they were closer to the fishing boats that could be seen in the distance, tossed like leaves in the storm. The mermaids reached the fleet and, according to the story that Soleil told for the rest of her life, they guided the boats through a channel in the waves that should not have existed. A path of calmer water, no wider than a single boat, that led directly to the harbor at Sandy Point.

One by one, the boats came in. They were battered and soaked, the men exhausted and terrified, but they were alive. Every boat returned. Every man survived.

When the last boat touched the harbor wall, the sea went quiet as suddenly as it had risen. The waves smoothed. The sky lightened. And near the Black Rocks, the mermaids surfaced one final time, their heads above the water, their eyes fixed on the shore. Then they dove, and the villagers say they have not been seen at the surface since.

Mama Vivienne lived another twenty years after that storm. She told Soleil, and Soleil told her children, and the story became part of the fabric of the village. The mermaids of Black Rocks, she said, were not simple creatures. They were ancient and complex, capable of destruction and of mercy. The key was respect. Those who respected the sea might find, when the worst came, that the sea respected them in return.
themes: the unexpected mercy of feared spirits
moral: The forces we fear are not always our enemies. Respect the sea, honor the old stories, and you may find that what you feared becomes your salvation.

title: Moko Jumbie: The Tall Guardian
summary: On the night before a village festival, a young stilt-walker named Corwin learns why the Moko Jumbie towers above the rooftops — not for spectacle, but to see the spirits that creep toward the sleeping village.
full_text:
The festival of Notting Hill was still a week away, but in the village of Chateaubelair the preparations had already begun. Corwin Baptiste, who was sixteen and lanky as a breadfruit sapling, had been chosen to walk on stilts for the first time. His uncle, Master Raymond, was the village's oldest Moko Jumbie, and he had spent three evenings teaching Corwin to balance on bamboo poles that raised him seven feet above the earth.

'You think this is about dancing,' Master Raymond said, wiping clay from his hands. 'It is not about dancing. The height is the point. When you are up there, you see what others cannot. You see what comes.'

Corwin did not understand. He thought the stilts were tradition, a spectacle, something tourists photographed and children cheered. He had never considered that the towering figure might serve a purpose beyond carnival.

The night before the festival, a storm rolled in from the Atlantic — not a proper hurricane, but a thick, wet darkness that pressed against the windows and made the candles gutter. Corwin lay in his hammock listening to the wind rattle the zinc roof when he heard a sound that did not belong to the storm. It was a low, rhythmic tapping, like a walking stick on packed earth, and it was coming from the road.

He rose and went to the window. The moon had broken through the clouds, and in its pale light he saw a figure moving down the road on stilts. It was impossibly tall — taller than any man on poles had a right to be — and it moved with a slow, deliberate gait that shook the ground with each step. The figure wore a headdress of shells and raffia that clicked and whispered in the wind, and its body was draped in layers of cloth that caught the moonlight and threw it back in fragments.

Corwin knew what it was. Every child in Saint Vincent knew. The Moko Jumbie.

But this was not Master Raymond. This was something older, something that had walked these roads long before the village existed. The figure stopped beneath Corwin's window and turned its head — if a mask could turn — and looked directly at him. He felt the gaze like a hand pressed to his chest.

Then the Moko Jumbie lifted one stilt and pointed down the road, toward the cluster of houses where families slept. Corwin followed the gesture and saw, or thought he saw, a shadow moving between the houses. It was not the shadow of a cloud or a tree. It moved against the wind, low to the ground, and where it passed, the dogs whimpered and went silent.

The Moko Jumbie began to walk toward it. Each step was slow and enormous, and with every stride the shell headdress rang like a bell. The shadow froze, then recoiled. It gathered itself and fled toward the sea, dissolving into the darkness like smoke into water.

The Moko Jumbie stood at the edge of the village and watched it go. Then it turned back, looked once more at Corwin, and walked — walked upward, as though the air were solid — until it was gone.

In the morning, Corwin told Master Raymond what he had seen. The old man nodded slowly and handed him the stilts.

'Now you understand,' he said. 'The Moko Jumbie does not walk for the crowd. The Moko Jumbie walks for the village. The height is not pride. It is vigilance. You see evil before it arrives, and you stand tall enough that it knows it has been seen.'

That afternoon, Corwin walked on stilts for the festival, and the crowd cheered and the music played. But his eyes were not on the dancers below. They were on the rooftops, the roads, the spaces between houses where shadows pooled. He walked tall, and he watched, and he understood at last what the old tradition meant — that the tallest figure in the village was not a performer but a sentinel, a guardian raised above the world so that no harm could approach unseen.
moral: True guardianship is not spectacle but vigilance — to stand above the crowd is to see what the crowd cannot, and to bear that sight is a sacred responsibility.

title: Rounces: The Night Riders
summary: A fisherman who mocks his grandmother's warnings about the Rounces discovers that the spirit-animals which ride the sleeping have their own terrible logic, and that the paralysis they bring is not cruelty but a test of the soul.
full_text:
Old Celia Baptiste had rules about sleep. She told her grandchildren every time they stayed at her house in Georgetown: do not sleep on your back, do not sleep with your feet pointing toward the door, and if you wake and cannot move, do not fight. Let it pass. Say nothing. Breathe.

Her grandson Derek, who was fourteen and thought his grandmother superstitious, broke all three rules on the same night.

It happened during the mango season, when the air was so thick with the sweetness of overripe fruit that even breathing felt like eating. Derek had eaten too much, slept too late, and fallen asleep on his back with his feet toward the door because the room was small and the hammock swung that way. He dreamed of nothing at all, and then he was awake — or believed he was.

He could not move. His arms were at his sides, his legs straight, his head turned slightly to the left. He could see the room: the candle guttering on the shelf, the gecko frozen on the wall, the moonlight coming through the window in a blade. He could hear the tree frogs and the distant thump of a bass drum from some party in the hills. But he could not lift a finger or turn his head or make any sound at all.

Then he felt the weight. It began at his chest — a pressure, heavy and warm, as though something large had settled onto him. It was not painful, but it was absolute, and it was alive. He could feel it breathing, or perhaps it was his own breathing slowed and deepened until each inhale was a labour and each exhale a relief.

In the corner of his vision, something moved. It was not a person and not quite an animal. It was a shape, dark and indistinct, with the suggestion of limbs and the certainty of presence. It did not approach him. It sat in the corner of the room, watching, and its watching was a weight in itself.

Derek tried to fight. He strained against the paralysis with every muscle, and for his effort the weight on his chest doubled. He could not breathe. The room dimmed. The shape in the corner leaned forward, and he felt something that was not quite fear and not quite understanding — a recognition that this was not punishment but something older and more impersonal, like weather.

He stopped fighting. He let the weight settle. He breathed as his grandmother had instructed — slowly, deeply, without thought. The pressure eased. The shape in the corner sat back. Time passed in a way that had nothing to do with clocks.

When morning came, Derek was on his side, facing the wall, and the room was empty and bright. He lay there for a long time, listening to the roosters and the sea. Then he went to his grandmother and told her everything.

Old Celia nodded. 'The Rounces ride those who sleep with their doors open,' she said. 'They are not evil. They test. They press the chest to see if the spirit is strong enough to bear weight. You fought, and it nearly crushed you. You yielded, and it passed.'

'What are they?' Derek asked.

'Spirit-animals. Old things. They come from the time before people named them. Some say they are the restless shadows of animals that died in the forests. Some say they are something else entirely. It does not matter what they are. What matters is that you know the rules: sleep on your side, keep your feet from the door, and when they come, do not fight. Let them ride. Let them pass.'

Derek slept on his side for the rest of that visit. He kept his feet from the door. And though he felt the Rounces twice more before he left — the pressure, the weight, the watching — he did not fight, and each time the sensation faded like a tide going out, leaving him whole and breathing in the dark.
moral: Some battles are won not by fighting but by knowing when to yield; the spirits that ride the sleeping are not conquerors but testers of the soul's endurance.

title: Rounce: The Forest Keeper
summary: A timber cutter who defies the old prohibition against felling trees in the deep forest encounters the Rounce, a nature spirit that punishes those who take more than they need and rewards those who leave offerings of respect.
full_text:
In the interior of Saint Vincent, where the volcanic mountains rise so steeply that the clouds snag on their peaks, there is a forest that the old people call the Green Keep. It is dense and ancient and full of sounds that do not belong to birds or wind. The villagers of Fancy and Georgetown have always known about the Green Keep, and they have always known the rule: take what you need, leave an offering, and never cut the great trees that the Rounce has chosen as its own.

Gideon Charles was a timber man who had cut wood in every forest on the island. He was not cruel, but he was practical, and practical men do not believe in spirits that live in trees. When the hurricane of 1987 flattened half the plantations and the demand for building timber doubled, Gideon took his axe into the Green Keep.

He had been there before, at the edges, but never deep. The deeper forest was different. The canopy was so thick that noon was twilight, and the air was cool and wet and smelled of moss and old wood. The trees were enormous — mombin, mahogany, bulletwood — their trunks wider than a man's armspan, their roots crawling over the ground like sleeping serpents.

Gideon marked a tree and swung his axe. The sound was wrong. Instead of the clean ring of steel on wood, there was a thud, as though he had struck something soft. He looked at the blade. It was dull, as though he had been cutting stone. He sharpened it and struck again. The same thud, the same dull blade.

Then the forest went quiet. Not gradually, as a forest quiets at dusk, but all at once, as though a hand had been pressed over every throat. The birds stopped. The insects stopped. Even the wind stopped. And in that silence, Gideon heard breathing that was not his own.

He turned. Standing between two mahogany trees was a figure that was not a figure. It had the shape of a man, but it was made of the forest — bark and vine and fungus and the dark, rich soil of the forest floor. Its eyes were knots in a plank of wood, and its hands were branches, and its voice, when it spoke, was the sound of a tree falling in a place where no one is listening.

'You cut without asking. You take without giving. You do not hear the forest because you have never listened.'

Gideon was not a man who frightened easily, but his legs failed him and he sat down heavily on the root of the tree he had been cutting. 'I meant no harm,' he said, and was surprised to find that it was true.

The Rounce — for that is what the old people would have called it — moved closer. Where it walked, the ground did not dent. It reached out one branch-hand and touched the axe. The steel flaked away like ash.

'The forest gives,' the Rounce said. 'It gives wood and fruit and shade and the breath you are breathing now. It gives without being asked. But the one who takes must also give. A seed. A word. A moment of stillness. You gave nothing. You brought only the axe.'

Gideon understood. He reached into his pocket and took out a handful of seeds — breadfruit seeds he carried to plant in cleared land. He set them on the ground at the base of the tree.

The Rounce looked at the seeds for a long time. Then it stepped back, and the forest sounds returned — tentatively at first, then in a rush, as though a door had been opened.

'Leave,' the Rounce said. 'Take your axe and your seeds and leave. Plant the seeds at the forest's edge. Let the forest grow outward. That is your offering.'

Gideon left the Green Keep that day and never cut timber there again. He planted the seeds at the forest's edge, and they grew into trees that are there still, tall and straight at the border between the wild and the cleared. And when the old people of Fancy tell the story of the Rounce, they tell it with Gideon's name, and they say that the forest keeper is still there, still breathing, still listening for the sound of an axe in a place where no axe should be.
themes: the cost of taking without giving
moral: The forest gives freely, but the one who takes without giving back will face the keeper of what remains; true wealth is not in what you cut but in what you leave standing.

title: Soucouyant: The Fire in the Dark
summary: A young woman who dismisses the old protective rituals of salt and garlic discovers the Soucouyant is real when she sees a ball of fire cross the yard and finds her baby's cribside stained with ash.
full_text:
In the hills above Georgetown, in a house with blue shutters and a zinc roof that sang in the rain, there lived a young mother named Lucille. She had a baby boy, three months old, with eyes like polished river stones and a cry that could wake the dead. Lucille loved him fiercely, but she was modern. She had been to the secondary school. She had read books. She did not believe in Soucouyant.

Her mother, Miss Anise, believed. Miss Anise kept a line of salt across every doorway and hung garlic above the baby's crib. She sprinkled salt on the windowsills and placed a pair of open scissors beneath the baby's mattress. When Lucille asked why, Miss Anise said, 'Because the Soucouyant rides at night, and if she finds a way in, she will feed on the child.'

Lucille smiled and said nothing. She thought the rituals were superstition, the residue of an ignorant age. She let the salt blow away in the wind. She threw out the garlic because it smelled. She removed the scissors because they were a choking hazard.

Three nights after she removed the protections, she woke to a sound. It was not a cry and not a footstep. It was a crackling, like a fire burning in a dry field, and it was coming from outside her window.

She rose and looked out. The yard was silver with moonlight, and there, hovering above the guava tree, was a ball of fire. It was the size of a coconut, bright orange, and it moved with a purpose that fire does not have. It drifted toward the house, leaving a trail of heat that Lucille could feel through the glass.

She froze. Every instinct told her to slam the window shut, but her hands would not obey. The fire-ball paused at the window frame, and for a moment she saw — or imagined she saw — a face within the flame. It was old and sharp and female, with eyes that burned not with light but with hunger.

Then it was gone, slipping through the gap between the window and the frame as though it were smoke.

Lucille ran to the baby's room. He was asleep, his chest rising and falling with the steady rhythm of the innocent. But the crib sheet was warm to the touch, and on the edge of the mattress there was a circle of ash, still faintly smoking, and the smell — acrid, animal, ancient — was the smell of something that should not have been there.

She did not sleep that night. She sat in the chair by the crib, a knife in one hand and a Bible in the other, and she watched the door until dawn.

In the morning, Miss Anise came with fresh salt and new garlic and a bundle of dried herbs that she burned in every room. She did not say I told you so. She simply did what needed to be done, and when it was done, she sat with Lucille on the veranda and drank cocoa tea and said:

'The Soucouyant is not a story for children. She is a woman who learned the old Obeah, the fire-reading, the skin-shedding. By day she is old and harmless. By night she sheds her skin and flies, and she feeds — not to kill, but to take. The blood of the young gives her another year. That is her bargain with whatever darkness she made it with.'

'Is she gone?' Lucille asked.

'She will not come while the salt is down and the garlic hangs. But you must keep the protections. Not because you believe. Because the child is here, and she is out there, and belief has nothing to do with it.'

Lucille kept the protections after that. She salted every doorway herself. She hung the garlic. She placed the scissors beneath the mattress. And on moonlit nights when the air smelled of overripe fruit and old fire, she closed the windows and sat with her baby and did not look outside, because she knew — now, with the certainty of one who has seen — that the ball of fire was real, and it was patient, and it would come again.
moral: The protections of the old ways were not born of ignorance but of knowledge that the modern world has chosen to forget; to discard them is to stand naked before what they held at bay.

title: Haggs: The Twilight Wanderer
summary: A schoolteacher new to the island dismisses the village warnings about the Haggs, a malevolent spirit of the twilight hours, until she finds her classroom filled with the scent of burning herbs and the chalk has written itself on the board.
full_text:
Miss Rowena Clarke arrived in Saint Vincent in the wet season of 1994, sent by the ministry to teach at a small primary school in the village of Troumaca. She was from Kingstown, a city woman, and she regarded the rural villages with a mixture of fondness and pity, the way one regards a relative who still believes in the old ways.

The school was a single building with three classrooms, a rusted flagpole, and a yard that turned to ankle-deep mud when the rains came. The children were bright and quick, and Rowena liked them immediately. But the villagers were reserved in a way that puzzled her. They were polite, even warm, but there were subjects they would not discuss, and one of them was the Haggs.

She first heard the word from an old woman named Miss Priscilla, who swept the schoolyard each morning. 'You must not stay after dark,' Miss Priscilla said, her broom beating the ground with emphasis. 'The Haggs comes at twilight. It walks the roads and the schoolyard and the churchyard. It brings bad luck to those who see it, and worse luck to those who do not look away.'

Rowena thanked her and thought nothing more of it. She was a woman of education and reason, and she did not believe in spirits that walked at twilight.

But the warnings continued. The headmaster, Mr. Charles, asked her politely to lock the classroom by six. The parents of her students asked if she could arrange dismissal before the evening bell. Even the children whispered about the Haggs, though they fell silent whenever she asked them what they meant.

One evening in late October, Rowena stayed late to grade papers. The classroom was small and hot, and the ceiling fan made a sound like a slow heartbeat. She worked by the light of a single bulb, and when she looked up, the sky outside the window had turned the colour of a bruise — purple and grey and deepening toward black.

She gathered her papers and stood to leave. Then the light flickered. It did not go out; it wavered, as though something had passed between the bulb and the room, and in that moment the air changed. It grew cool and heavy, and with it came a smell — thick, herbal, like sage and smoke and something older, something that had no name in Rowena's vocabulary.

The chalk on the blackboard moved. She watched it — actually watched it — as a word appeared in her own handwriting, or a close imitation of it: LEAVE.

Rowena did not leave. She stood very still and looked at the word and felt, for the first time in her adult life, a fear that was not of the dark or of the unknown but of the certainty that something was in the room with her and that it was not human. It was not an animal. It was a presence, a weight in the air, a wrongness that pressed against her thoughts and made them scatter like chickens in a rain.

She picked up the chalk and wrote beneath the first word: WHO ARE YOU?

The answer appeared instantly, the letters jagged and sharp: HAGGS.

Then the light steadied, the smell faded, and the room was empty. Rowena stood there for a long time, her hands shaking, her papers on the floor. When she finally locked the door and walked home, the twilight was over and the stars were out, and she did not look at the shadows between the houses.

She never stayed late again. She locked the classroom by five-thirty and walked home with the other teachers, and when Miss Priscilla told her stories about the Haggs — how it came on Hop-tu-Naa nights and festival eves, how it brought misfortune and madness to those who provoked it — Rowena listened. She did not argue. She did not explain. She had seen the word on the board, and she knew that some things do not require belief to be real.

Years later, when she had become one of the old teachers that the new ones came to for advice, she would tell them the same thing Miss Priscilla had told her: do not stay after dark, do not walk the roads at twilight, and if the chalk writes on the board by itself, do not answer it. Leave. Lock the door. Come back in the morning, when the Haggs has gone back to wherever the Haggs goes when the sun is high.
moral: Knowledge of the world comes not only from books but from the places where books have not yet gone; to dismiss the warnings of those who have seen what you have not is not wisdom but arrogance.

title: Mahogany Tree, the Sacred Sentinel
summary: The sacred mahogany tree of Antigua is believed to be inhabited by a powerful guardian spirit who protects the island's forests and punishes those who harm them.
full_text:
On the island of Antigua, the mahogany tree is more than timber. It is a living spirit, a guardian of the land. The old people say that when the first mahogany tree sprouted on the island, a spirit of the earth entered its roots and made it its home. That spirit has watched over the forests ever since. The mahogany tree grows tall and straight, its bark dark and deeply furrowed, its leaves spreading like a canopy over the smaller trees beneath. It is the king of the forest, and it knows every creature within its domain.

To cut down a mahogany tree without permission is to invite misfortune. Fishermen tell of a man who felled a great mahogany on the northeastern coast to build a boat. The boat was launched, but it never returned. Some say it was caught in a squall. Others say the spirit of the mahogany pulled it beneath the waves. After that, the islanders began asking the tree's permission before cutting. They would leave a small offering of rum and sugar at its base and explain their need. If the offering was accepted, the tree would fall cleanly. If rejected, the saw would bind or the weather would turn.

To this day, many Antiguan homes have a mahogany tree planted in the yard, not for its shade but for its protection. The spirit within keeps away evil, blesses the family, and ensures that the land remains fruitful.
moral: Respect for nature brings blessings; greed brings ruin.

title: Soucouyant, the Antiguan Fireball
summary: A fearsome vampire of the Caribbean, the Soucouyant sheds her skin by night and flies as a fireball to suck the blood of her victims.
full_text:
In the islands of Antigua and Barbuda, the Soucouyant is the most dreaded of all spirits. She appears by day as an old woman, often a neighbor or a grandmother, indistinguishable from anyone else. But when darkness falls, she removes her wrinkled skin and hides it in a mortar, then transforms into a ball of fire that flies through the night, searching for victims. She enters homes through keyholes or cracks in the walls and drains the blood of the sleeping.

Those who wake to find themselves weak and pale know the Soucouyant has visited. The only defense is to scatter rice or seeds around the house; the Soucouyant will be compelled to count every grain before she can enter, and dawn will catch her before she finishes. Another method is to find her skin where she has hidden it and sprinkle salt or pepper inside it. When she returns, the burning sensation will force her to reveal herself.

A famous cautionary tale tells of a man who married a beautiful woman from another village. Every morning he woke exhausted, his blood drained. A wise obeah woman advised him to stay awake and watch. That night he saw his wife remove her skin and fly away as a flame. The next day he confronted her, and she fled into the forest, never to be seen again. The villagers searched but found only the burned remains of a fireball. The man learned that appearances can be deceiving, and that evil sometimes wears a beautiful face.
moral: Do not be deceived by appearances; evil often wears a familiar face.

title: Jumbie, the Restless Spirit
summary: In Antiguan folklore, a Jumbie is a restless spirit of the dead that haunts the living, often appearing at crossroads or near ancient trees.
full_text:
Throughout the Caribbean, the word Jumbie strikes fear into those who hear it. In Antigua, the Jumbie is a spirit of the dead who has not moved on to the next world. It lingers because of unfinished business, a buried secret, or a violent death. The Jumbie can appear in many forms: a shadow at the corner of your eye, a cold breath on your neck, a tapping on your window at midnight. But its true form, glimpsed only by the brave, is that of a tall, dark figure with hollow eyes and skeletal hands.

Jumbies are most active at crossroads, at midnight, and during the full moon. They cannot cross running water, and they are repelled by the smell of burning sage or the sound of church bells. A Jumbie may follow a traveler home and haunt their house, causing objects to move, lights to flicker, and sleep to be troubled. The only way to be rid of a Jumbie is to discover what keeps it tied to the world of the living and resolve that matter.

An old story from the village of Liberta tells of a Jumbie that haunted a particular silk cotton tree. Villagers heard weeping at night, and livestock would not go near the tree. An elder consulted the spirits and learned that the Jumbie was a woman who had been buried without proper rites generations ago. The village held a proper funeral, said the prayers, and the weeping stopped. The tree became peaceful once more, and travelers now rest in its shade without fear. The Jumbie had finally found its rest.
moral: Even the dead deserve peace and proper respect.

title: Dutchman, the Guyanese Phantom
summary: The ghost of a Dutch colonist who wanders the plantations and canals of Guyana, forever searching for the treasure he buried and never reclaimed.
full_text:
In the riverside villages of Guyana, where the canals still bear the marks of Dutch engineering, there is a ghost that has been seen for three centuries. The Dutchman is what his name suggests: the spirit of a Dutch colonist, dressed in 17th-century clothing, a tricorn hat on his head, a clay pipe in his mouth. He walks the old plantations at dusk, carrying a lantern that flickers with an unnatural blue flame.

The Dutchman is searching. Before he died, he buried a chest of gold coins somewhere along the Demerara River. He intended to return for it, but fever took him first. Now his spirit cannot rest until the treasure is found. He appears to those who are alone and desperate, beckoning them to follow. Those who follow the Dutchman find themselves walking for hours, lost in familiar places, until they collapse from exhaustion. The ghost does not harm them. He simply wants company in his endless search.

A sugar worker named Ramjohn once encountered the Dutchman near a canal. The ghost pointed to a spot beneath a cotton tree. Ramjohn dug and found a small leather pouch containing a few silver coins, not the treasure chest of legend. 'Take them,' the ghost seemed to whisper. 'Tell others I am still waiting.' Ramjohn took the coins to the village elder, who said the Dutchman was not a ghost to be feared but a soul to be pitied. The money was donated to the church, and the congregation prayed for the Dutchman's rest. Whether he found peace or still walks the canals, no one can say. But the people of Guyana know to be polite if they see a man in old Dutch clothes, smoking a pipe with a blue flame.
moral: Some souls are bound to the earth by nothing more than unfinished business.

title: Ole Higue, the Guyanese Vampire
summary: A vampire-like spirit of Guyanese folklore, the Ole Higue is an old woman who sheds her skin at night and flies as a ball of light to drink blood.
full_text:
The Ole Higue is one of the most feared spirits in Guyana. She appears as a harmless old woman by day, perhaps a neighbor, perhaps a grandmother. But at night, she removes her skin and hides it in a mortar, then transforms into a ball of fire or a glowing light that flies through the darkness. The Ole Higue enters homes through the smallest openings and drinks the blood of sleeping victims, especially children and infants.

The signs of an Ole Higue attack are unmistakable. The victim wakes exhausted, pale, with tiny marks on their neck or chest. Children become listless and weak. In severe cases, they waste away and die. The only defense is vigilance and the old remedies: placing a broom upside down behind the door, scattering rice or sand that the Higue must count before entering, or finding her hidden skin and filling it with salt and pepper.

A farmer in Berbice suspected his elderly neighbor was an Ole Higue when his children began wasting away. He stayed awake one night and saw a ball of light enter the children's room. The next day, he searched the neighbor's yard until he found a mortar hidden beneath a bush. Inside was a wrinkled, empty skin. He knew the old stories: fill the skin with salt and pepper, and the Higue will be unable to re-enter it without burning. He did so. That night, the ball of light returned to the mortar, but it could not re-enter its skin. The following morning, the old woman was found dead, her body covered in burns. The children recovered. The story spread, and the people of Guyana still take precautions against the Ole Higue, a reminder that evil sometimes lives right next door.
moral: Evil often wears a familiar face; vigilance is the price of safety.

title: Backoo, the Barnacle Spirit
summary: A mischievous water spirit of Guyanese folklore, the Backoo is a small, hairy creature covered in barnacles that lives in rivers and canals.
full_text:
In the rivers and canals of Guyana, there lives a peculiar creature called the Backoo. It is small, about the size of a child, with a body covered in shaggy black hair and encrusted with barnacles and river moss. Its eyes are large and yellow, like an owl's, and its fingers are long and webbed. The Backoo is not evil, but it is mischievous. It delights in hiding the belongings of fishermen, tangling their nets, and stealing the fish from their lines.

The Backoo cannot speak, but it understands human speech. It responds to kindness and cruelty in equal measure. A fisherman who shares his catch with the Backoo, leaving a few small fish on the riverbank, will find his nets full the next day. A fisherman who curses the Backoo or tries to catch it will find his lines tangled, his boat leaking, his luck vanished.

A young fisherman named Devon once caught a Backoo in his net. He was horrified at first, but the creature looked at him with such pitiful eyes that he could not harm it. He gently untangled the Backoo and released it back into the water. The Backoo surfaced, nodded once, and disappeared. From that day, Devon's nets were always the fullest. He became the wealthiest fisherman on the Essequibo Coast. When asked his secret, he would smile and say nothing. But those who knew him understood: he had made a friend in the water. The Backoo still lives in the canals of Guyana, a reminder that even the strangest creatures deserve compassion and that kindness is always rewarded.
moral: Kindness to the smallest creature brings the greatest rewards.

title: The Chureca, the Virgin Islands Beast
summary: A fearsome beast of the Virgin Islands, the Chureca is a monstrous creature that emerges from the forest to devour livestock and threaten villagers.
full_text:
In the Virgin Islands, when the goats go missing and the dogs refuse to venture into the hills, the old people say: 'The Chureca is hunting.' The Chureca is a beast of legend, a creature of the deep forest that defies easy description. Some say it is a giant dog with red eyes. Others say it is a misshapen bull with hooves that leave no tracks. All agree on one thing: the Chureca is hungry.

The Chureca comes down from the hills when food is scarce in the forest. It raids chicken coops, carries off goats, and has been known to attack humans who venture too close to its lair. Farmers on St. Thomas and St. John have told stories for generations about the beast that kills silently and vanishes into the bush. No one has ever caught the Chureca, though many have tried.

A farmer on St. Croix once set a trap for the Chureca after losing half his flock. He built a strong pen and baited it with a young goat. That night, he heard a commotion and rushed out with his lantern. The pen was destroyed, the goat was gone, and the trap was sprung but empty. In the mud, he saw tracks unlike any he had ever seen: cloven hooves the size of his hand, spaced far apart as if the creature had taken enormous leaps. The farmer fortified his fences and accepted his losses. The Chureca was smarter than any trap, and some forces of nature cannot be defeated, only endured.
moral: Nature's wildness cannot be tamed; learn to live with it.
source: Virgin Islands oral tradition, Caribbean folklore
